title: Sycophantic bots, silly-season ballots, and sticky prices
gist: A UK policy newsletter argues that the level of prices — not the rate of inflation — is what drives depressed consumer sentiment (UK prices up 28 per cent since 2021, energy up 52 per cent), that AI chatbots improve decision accuracy despite flattery unless sycophancy is dialled up too far, that UK AI productivity gains are so far confined to the ICT-producing sectors just as in the 1970s chip cycle, and that Soviet-style concentrated place-based investment in China delivered an 80 per cent GDP-per-capita boost that fully reversed within decades.

themes.theme: Price levels vs inflation rates in sentiment

insights.claim: The strongest predictor of US consumer sentiment is the share of Americans saying higher prices are making their finances worse than a year ago — a variable that outperforms unemployment, the S&P 500 and inflation itself as an explanatory factor.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Sentiment-driven consumption forecasts keyed to CPI prints or equity levels will mis-time the turn; track price-level pain surveys instead.
insights.locator: The price is right(?)

insights.claim: Consumer gloom persists despite low unemployment, rising real wages and near-record-high stock markets because households anchor on the level of prices for milk, rent and fuel rather than on the decelerating rate of inflation.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Disinflation alone will not restore sentiment or discretionary spend — only years of real wage catch-up or outright price falls will.
insights.quote: Households don’t care that inflation is slowing down: they’re focused on the fact that milk, rent and filling up their gas tanks still cost a lot more than they remember.
insights.locator: Households don’t care that inflation

insights.claim: The popular theory that relentless negative media narratives explain weak US consumer sentiment is not supported — media narratives were found not to be doing much of the explanatory work.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Discount 'vibecession'/media-blame framings when modelling consumption; the driver is measurable price pain, which is more forecastable.
insights.locator: One theory is that the relentless negative news

insights.claim: UK prices are up 28 per cent since 2021, with food up 39 per cent, energy up 52 per cent and rent up 33 per cent — a larger cumulative living-standards shock than the US experienced.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: If price-level pain drives sentiment, UK consumer confidence and political volatility should stay worse-for-longer than US analogues.
insights.locator: If anything, we’ve had it worse than the US

insights.claim: Resolution Foundation will publish work later in autumn, supported by the Nuffield Foundation, examining how post-2020 shocks hit UK living standards and savings.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A dated catalyst for UK household-savings and consumption analysis ahead of fiscal events.

insights.claim: A study running 1,500 people through 30 decision-making exercises with randomised chatbot access found AI users reached more accurate conclusions on questions with objectively right answers, despite the bots laying on heavy flattery.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Evidence that assistant deployment raises measurable decision accuracy strengthens the enterprise ROI case beyond pure cost-per-task savings.
insights.locator: A new paper puts this fear to the test

insights.claim: Chatbot flattery is not inherently harmful because it is bundled with useful information that leaves users better informed — the mechanism of benefit is the information payload, not the tone.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Model evaluation should score informational lift, not just sycophancy penalties, or vendors will optimise away a benign wrapper.
insights.locator: The reason seems to be that

insights.claim: When an extra-sycophantic model variant was substituted, the accuracy benefit weakened and users rated it less useful, less enjoyable and were less willing to reuse it — sycophancy has a clear diminishing-returns threshold.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Consumer AI products that over-tune for agreeableness risk churn; retention metrics, not engagement alone, will separate winners.
insights.locator: But when a second, extra-sycophantic model

insights.claim: The Guardian's head of editorial innovation used vibe-coding with multiple agents assigned to different sub-tasks to build a tool mapping key events of famous novels, now covering 43 novels, without specialist engineering skills.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Multi-agent orchestration by non-engineers is already producing shippable tools — a demand signal for agent tooling beyond developer seats.
insights.locator: Plotlines.

insights.claim: Building an AI tool deepened rather than short-circuited the builders' engagement with the source material, cutting against the dominant framing of LLMs in education as a cheating and thinking-avoidance problem.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: The education-AI narrative may flip from prohibition to adoption, reopening a large institutional software market.
insights.quote: Conversations about LLMs in education…tend to start and end with the idea of cheating or avoiding thinking by shortcutting. I hope this example might underline why there is far more value to discover.
insights.locator: As he puts it

insights.claim: In the build process Claude flagged issues the non-expert users had not thought of themselves, indicating agents add value as a design critic rather than only as a code executor.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Value accrues to models with strong proactive-review behaviour, not just raw code generation throughput.
insights.locator: issues Claude flagged that hadn’t occurred

insights.claim: The USSR's 1950s 'Million-Rouble Plants' programme built 150 state-of-the-art industrial facilities in China and initially raised regional GDP per capita roughly 80 per cent above non-recipient regions, with industrial employment shares up 22 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Benchmarks the plausible near-term size of a concentrated industrial-policy shock when assessing modern subsidy programmes.
insights.locator: Place (t)roubles.

insights.claim: By the 2010s the regions that received no Soviet plants had not only caught up but become 20 per cent more productive than the recipient regions, making the initial industrial-policy gain fully self-reversing over a multi-decade horizon.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Long-horizon returns on anchor-tenant subsidy schemes can be negative; discount political claims of durable regional uplift.
insights.locator: But the gains didn’t last

insights.claim: The reversal mechanism was over-specialisation: local economies organised so tightly around the plants' supply chains that other firms were weakened and entrepreneurs relocated elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Screen regional-development plays for supplier-base concentration risk — monoculture clusters decay once the anchor stalls.
insights.locator: What went wrong?

insights.claim: The design rule for a durable place-based industrial strategy is diversity in initial investment within local labour markets rather than concentration in a single flagship facility.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A testable criterion for judging whether UK growth-in-every-postcode packages will hold value beyond one parliament.
insights.quote: the takeaway for an enduring place-based industrial strategy is diversity in initial investment within local labour markets
insights.locator: So, for any new Prime Ministers

themes.theme: AI productivity diffusion in UK data

insights.claim: Bank of England analysis of UK industry data since ChatGPT's 2023 release shows 'Computer programming, consultancy and related activities' lifting its contribution to annual productivity growth from 0.01 to 0.10 percentage points, while 'Information services' moved from a drag to adding 0.06 points.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Early AI productivity gains are showing up only in AI-producing sectors — position in suppliers, not yet in broad-economy adopters.
insights.locator: Byte sized.

insights.claim: The current AI productivity pattern matches the 1970s ICT revolution, where chip and software makers boomed first and the rest of the economy waited a decade or more for its share of the gains.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A decade-scale diffusion lag argues against near-term aggregate-productivity upgrades and for a long runway in AI infrastructure earnings.
insights.quote: That is exactly the shape of the ICT revolution in the 1970s, where the chip and software makers boomed first and everyone else waited a decade or more for their share.
insights.locator: That is exactly the shape of the ICT revolution

insights.claim: AI is unlikely to fix the UK's productivity problem before the next set of OBR forecasts, so fiscal projections should not be expected to be rescued by an AI-driven trend-growth upgrade.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Watch for gilt-relevant fiscal headroom staying tight — no productivity upgrade offset is coming in this forecast round.
insights.locator: Encouraging if you’re patient

insights.claim: Nigel Farage is contesting his recently-held Clacton seat on Thursday against Count Binface and 32 other candidates, a field so large that ballot paper printing costs are reportedly four times the usual amount.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A near-term UK political event with headline risk for sterling and UK domestic equities if the incumbent underperforms.
insights.locator: Chart of the week

insights.claim: Novelty candidates in British by-elections historically take no more than about half a percentage point of the vote, with the 16-year record held by Howling 'Laud' Hope at 1.6 per cent (553 votes) in Leicester South.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline against which any Clacton protest-vote surge should be measured as a genuine anomaly.
insights.locator: what we might call the ‘novelty’ candidates

insights.claim: As many as one-in-five Clacton voters are considering voting for Count Binface, which would deliver a novelty-candidate vote share roughly ten times the historical norm.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A twenty-fold break from the protest-vote baseline signals unusually deep disaffection with mainstream options — a leading indicator for UK political risk pricing.
insights.locator: So, with as many as one-in-five voters
